To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a significant proportion (approximately 30%) of the Greek cancer caregiver population has elevated informational needs, which are negatively associated with satisfaction and positively associated with preference for cancer-specific information.

a significant proportion (nearly 40%) of the caregivers had high needs for information and that their needs for information were positively associated with their preference (nearly 60%) for written information, negatively associated with their satisfaction with communication, negatively associated with affective behavior and not associated with anxiety or depression.

a significant proportion (about 50%) of the caregivers in our study experienced heightened levels of informational needs, which were positively correlated with a preference for printed material and negatively correlated with satisfaction with communication, while anxiety and depression were elevated and independent of the need of information or the preference for printed material.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the informational needs of primary Greek cancer caregivers and their psychological status, as well as the relationship between these two variables.
the needs, preferences, satisfaction and psychological status of the primary caregiver of cancer patients in the Greek oncological setting, and it is the first of its kind to be conducted in Greece.
the informational needs of primary Greek caregivers of cancer patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the oncologist should be aware of the informational needs of the caregiver, the preference for printed material and the level of satisfaction with communication, in order to provide the most effective care to both the cancer patient and his or her family.
the Greek caregiver needs more factual, disease specific, printed information, which is communicated in a sensitive and appropriate way by the oncologist.
the Greek cancer caregivers need more information about the disease and its treatment and they are not satisfied with the way they are informed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the oncology nurse should take into account the informational needs and the satisfaction of the primary caregiver, as well as the psychological distress, when caring for a cancer patient receiving chemotherapy.
Greek oncologists need to be more aware of the needs of their patients' caregivers. They should be able to detect their informational needs and to meet them.
the oncology team should be more aware of the informational needs and psychological distress of the Greek cancer caregiver, and should try to provide the necessary information in the best way.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the oncology nurse should be the first to assess the informational needs of the primary caregivers of cancer outpatients, to provide the appropriate information in a timely manner, and to refer those with elevated levels of psychological distress to the appropriate support services.
the Greek oncologist should not only try to identify the informational needs of the cancer caregiver, but should also possess the ability to meet them in a satisfactory way.
caregivers need more information about their loved one’s cancer and that the Greek doctor should try to identify their needs and provide the appropriate information in a satisfactory way.
